leads.text: SQL identifier injection in the runs filter compiler: the `field` value of a filter param, taken verbatim from the `GET /v1/runs` query string, is concatenated into a dynamic SQL identifier position via `sql(field + "_text")` at packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts:193 (sibling sites at the same file lines 202, 211, 217 and `sql(field + "_tokens")` at 243). Full chain: packages/backend/src/api/v1/runs/index.ts:68 `const queryString = ctx.querystring` -> :69 `deserializeLogic(queryString)` -> :73 `convertChecksToSQL(deserializedFilters)` -> packages/backend/src/checks/utils.ts:29 `runner.sql(logicElement.params)` -> checks/index.ts:190 `field = param1_5.field` -> :193 `sql(field + "_text")`; the resulting fragment is spliced raw into the outer query at runs/index.ts:88 `sql`... where r.project_id = ${projectId} ${parentRunFilter} and (${filtersQuery})``. Critically, the deserializer applies NO allowlist: packages/shared/filters/serialize.ts:30-49 `deserializeParamValue` returns bare `decodeURIComponent(v)` for both `select` and `text` param types, so `field` is never validated against the filter's declared option list. A verifier must confirm whether postgres.js `sql(<string>)` identifier escaping (double-quote doubling) fully neutralizes the concatenated value — if it does not, this is direct SQL injection into a SELECT on the `run` table.

leads.text: `sqlEval` is the highest-centrality SQL chokepoint in the backend and splices a caller-supplied fragment directly into a query body: packages/backend/src/checks/runChecks.ts:45 `const [result] = await tx`select * from temp_run where ${sqlFragment}``. Both callers pass attacker-derived fragments: runChecks.ts:91 `const snippet = runner.sql(params)` -> :93 `sqlEval(snippet, run)` (CandidateFlow rank 0, the top-ranked flow in the scan), and runChecks.ts:115 `const filterSql = convertChecksToSQL(checks)` -> :117 `sqlEval(filterSql, run)` (CandidateFlow rank 1). `params`/`checks` originate from user-controlled checklist/evaluation data (`checks = checklistData.data` at api/v1/evaluations/index.ts:122, persisted from the checklists API). Because `${sqlFragment}` is a nested postgres.js fragment it is interpolated as raw SQL text rather than a bound parameter, so any unparameterized text produced by the checks/index.ts fragment builders (see the `field`/`date` leads) executes here in a second, independent sink. `sqlEval` has centrality 4.19e-6 (highest of the 12 methods in the file) and reachable_from_entry=true at hop_distance 0, so a defect here has a large blast radius across every check-evaluation path.

leads.text: Attacker-controlled `date` filter param is interpolated inside a single-quoted SQL string literal rather than passed as a bound parameter: packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts:222 `sql`created_at ${postgresOperators(operator)} '${date}'``, where `date = param1_9.date` is assigned at line 221 from the filter params object that originates in the `GET /v1/runs` query string (same ctx.querystring -> deserializeLogic -> convertChecksToSQL -> runner.sql(params) chain as the `field` lead). leads.text: authMiddleware treats every path matching the unanchored regex /v1/datasets/.+ (and /v1/runs/.+/public, /v1/runs/.+/feedback, /auth/.+) as a "public route" and skips ALL authentication. On line 82 it unconditionally sets ctx.state.projectId from the attacker-controlled query string (ctx.request?.query?.projectId). The tenant-ownership control — `select id from project where id = ${ctx.state.projectId} and org_id = ${ctx.state.orgId}` on line 120, which throws "Project not found" — exists ONLY inside the authenticated branch (after verifyJwt on line 112). On the public-route branch (lines 90-105) there is no equivalent check: when isPublicRoute && !bearerToken, control falls straight to `await next()` on line 94 with projectId still equal to the raw query parameter. Therefore an unauthenticated request such as GET /v1/datasets/?projectId=<victim-project-uuid> with no Authorization header is served with the victim's projectId in ctx.state, and downstream handlers (e.g. datasets/index.ts:13 `select * from dataset d where project_id = ${projectId}`) trust it. Missing authorization/tenant-binding control on the public-route path.

Result (excerpts): line 62 `const publicRoutes = [new RegExp(`/auth/.+`), ..., new RegExp(`/v1/datasets/.+`), `/v1/evaluations/run`]`; line 82 `ctx.state.projectId = ctx.request?.query?.projectId as string`; line 90 `isPublicRoute && (!bearerToken || validateUUID(bearerToken))`; line 94 `await next()`; line 102 `ctx.state.projectId = bearerToken`; line 112 `verifyJwt<SessionData>(bearerToken)`; line 120 `sql`select id from project where id = ${ctx.state.projectId} and org_id = ${ctx.state.orgId}``; line 125 `new Error("Project not found")`. The org_id ownership check appears only once in the file, inside the post-verifyJwt branch.

leads.text: datasets.delete("/:id") performs `delete from dataset where id = ${id}` with NO `and project_id = ${projectId}` predicate and no ownership pre-check — unlike the sibling datasets.patch("/:id") on line 96 which DOES scope with `where id = ${id} and project_id = ${projectId}`. The handler does not even read projectId from ctx.state. Because /v1/datasets/<uuid> matches the publicRoutes regex `/v1/datasets/.+` in auth/utils.ts:62, this destructive route is reachable with no Authorization header at all, so any party who learns (or brute-forces) a dataset UUID can delete another tenant's dataset. Missing authorization control on a destructive route.

The /reset-password handler never validates the submitted token against the stored account.recovery_token column, and never invalidates it after use. /request-password-reset writes `update account set recovery_token = ${token} where id = ${user.id}` (auth/index.ts:180), but a graph-wide search shows recovery_token is NEVER read in any query in the repo — the column is write-only, so the intended single-use binding control is not enforced. /reset-password only calls verifyJwt<{email}>(token) (signature+exp) and then does `update account set password_hash = ${passwordHash} where email = ${email}`. Two consequences: (a) a reset token is infinitely replayable for its full lifetime; (b) because signJwt payloads carry no purpose/type/audience claim, ANY {email}-shaped JWT signed with JWT_SECRET is accepted as a password-reset token — including the email-confirmation token minted by `signJwt({ email })` at utils/emails.ts:14, which uses signJwt's default ONE_MONTH expiry (auth/utils.ts:32-33) rather than the ONE_HOUR used for resets. Missing token-binding / token-purpose-separation control.

projects.delete("/:projectId") takes projectId from ctx.params and deletes it with `delete from project where id = ${projectId}` — with NO predicate binding that project to the caller's org. The only check performed is a COUNT of the caller's own projects (`select count(*)::int from project where org_id = ${orgId}`, used solely to enforce "an organization must have at least one project"); that count never constrains WHICH project is deleted. Any authenticated user whose own org holds more than one project can therefore delete an arbitrary project belonging to any other organization by supplying its UUID. Missing resource-ownership authorization check.

projects.patch("/:projectId") takes projectId from ctx.params and runs `update project set name = ${name} where id = ${projectId}` with no org/tenant predicate whatsoever — the handler never even destructures orgId or projectId from ctx.state, so no ownership information is consulted. Any authenticated user can rename any project in any organization by UUID. Missing resource-ownership authorization check.

versions.patch("/:id") updates template_version content with `update template_version set content=..., extra=..., test_values=..., is_draft=... where id = ${ctx.params.id}` and no project_id/ownership predicate, and performs no prior lookup to confirm the version's parent template belongs to ctx.state.projectId. Every other template route in the codebase is scoped (e.g. templates.ts:85 `where project_id = ${ctx.state.projectId} and id = ${ctx.params.id}`), making this an isolated omission. Any authenticated user can overwrite another tenant's prompt template version — which the SDK then serves to that tenant's production LLM calls via the /v1/template_versions/latest route. Missing authorization check on a state-changing route.

runs.get("/:id/related") executes a RECURSIVE CTE seeded with `WHERE r1.id = ${id}` from ctx.params and returns rr.input, rr.output, rr.params, rr.feedback and rr.project_id for the whole run tree, with NO project_id or org_id predicate — the handler never reads ctx.state at all. Both sibling routes DO enforce scoping: runs.get("/:id") at line 189 scopes by orgId (with an explicit comment about teammates), and runs.get("/:id/feedback") at line 261 scopes by `project_id = ${projectId} and id = ${id}`. Any authenticated user can read another tenant's full LLM prompt/completion payloads by run UUID. Missing authorization check.

leads.text: The CORS policy reflects the caller's Origin verbatim while also enabling credentials, with no allowlist check anywhere. utils/cors.ts:7-9 sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: ctx.get("Origin") || "*"` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and the @koa/cors options at line 17 do the same via `origin(ctx) { return ctx.get("Origin") || "*" }` with `credentials: true`. Because corsMiddleware is registered globally at index.ts:33 (before authMiddleware at :34), any attacker-controlled web page can issue credentialed cross-origin reads of every API response. leads.text: No HTTP security-response-header control exists in either package. The backend's entire Koa middleware chain was fully enumerated (index.ts lines 29-43): requestHandler, tracingMiddleWare, errorMiddleware, logger(), corsMiddleware, authMiddleware, ratelimit, bodyParser(), setDefaultBody, then four routers — there is no helmet/koa-helmet or any header-setting middleware. The frontend's nextConfig object keys were likewise fully enumerated (next.config.js: reactStrictMode, eslint, typescript, images, rewrites, webpack, transpilePackages) — there is no `headers()` function. A repo-wide search for Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, helmet, csrf and SameSite returned zero rows. So the app ships with no CSP, no HSTS, no X-Frame-Options/clickjacking defence, no X-Content-Type-Options, and no CSRF token middleware.

leads.text: There is no brute-force / credential-stuffing protection on auth.post("/login") (auth/index.ts:139): the handler looks up the account by email and calls verifyPassword with no failed-attempt counter, no account lockout, and no per-account throttle. The only protection is the single global koa-ratelimit instance (index.ts:35), and that control is doubly weakened in utils/ratelimit.ts: (a) its `whitelist: (ctx) => { if (ctx.state.userId) return true; return false }` exempts every authenticated request from rate limiting entirely, and (b) its key is `id: (ctx) => ctx.request.ip || ctx.ip || ctx.state.userId` while index.ts:26 sets `app.proxy = true`, which makes Koa derive ctx.request.ip from the client-supplied X-Forwarded-For header — so an attacker can rotate that header to get a fresh 150-requests-per-minute bucket per forged value. Missing anti-automation control on authentication.

leads.text: versions.get("/:id") fetches the template_version by id with no ownership predicate (`select * from template_version where id = ${ctx.params.id}`) and then performs a SEPARATE scoped lookup for the parent template (`select * from template where project_id = ${ctx.state.projectId} and id = ${version.templateId}`) — but it never checks whether that second query returned anything before responding. It unconditionally returns `ctx.body = { ...version, template }`, so when the version belongs to another tenant the ownership query yields undefined for `template` while the full version row (including content and test_values) is still disclosed. The ownership check is performed but its result is never enforced.

redirections.post("/api/report") is registered in publicRoutes as the exact string "/api/report" (auth/utils.ts:64) and derives the target tenant entirely from the request body — `const projectId = events[0]?.projectId || events[0].app` — then calls processEventsIngestion(projectId, events) with no authentication of any kind and no verification that the caller holds a credential for that project. Unlike the modern ingest route (runs/ingest.ts:283) which reads projectId from ctx.state, this legacy route accepts the tenant identifier as untrusted body data, so anyone who learns a project UUID can inject arbitrary run/log records into that tenant's observability data. Missing authentication control on a write endpoint.

The Next.js image optimizer has no host restriction: next.config.js sets `images.remotePatterns = [{ protocol: "https", hostname: "**" }]`, a wildcard that permits any HTTPS host. The enumerated nextConfig keys contain no `domains` allowlist or any narrower pattern. This turns /_next/image into an open server-side fetch proxy — an unauthenticated attacker can supply arbitrary ?url= values to make the Next server issue outbound HTTPS requests to hosts of their choosing and reflect the responses. Missing remote-host allowlist control.

leads.text: In authMiddleware, the UUID validation protecting ctx.state.projectId is bypassed by a second, unguarded public-route branch. Line 90 guards the first branch with `isPublicRoute && (!bearerToken || validateUUID(bearerToken))` and only assigns projectId at line 92 after re-checking `validateUUID(bearerToken)`. Control reaches lines 99-102 precisely when the route is public AND a bearer token exists AND it is NOT a valid UUID — and that branch assigns `ctx.state.projectId = bearerToken` behind only a `typeof bearerToken === "string"` check, then calls `await next()` with no authentication. The whole function carries the hedge comment `// TODO: we need to refactor this / find a more elegant way to use this middleware because it doesn't make any sense what's hapenning here`, and line 82 additionally seeds `ctx.state.projectId` from the raw `ctx.request.query.projectId` before any auth runs. The org-ownership check (`select id from project where id = ${projectId} and org_id = ${orgId}`) only exists on the authenticated path, never on the public path. publicRoutes includes `new RegExp('/v1/datasets/.+')`, `/v1/runs/ingest`, `/v1/evaluations/run` and `new RegExp('/v1/runs/.+/feedback')`, and the handlers behind them read `const { projectId } = ctx.state` straight into SQL (e.g. `select * from dataset d where project_id = ${projectId}`), so an unauthenticated attacker chooses the tenant whose data is read/written.

leads.text: The global rate limiter in `packages/backend/src/utils/ratelimit.ts` is effectively neutralized along three independent axes, each marked by hedge/stale text. (1) The configured ceiling was raised to `max: 150` while the adjacent comment still reads `// limit unlogged IPs to 50 requests per minute` — the documented limit was tripled and the comment never updated, the classic signature of a quietly relaxed control. (2) `whitelist: (ctx) => { if (ctx.state.userId) return true; return false }` exempts every authenticated user from rate limiting entirely; because index.ts registers `app.use(authMiddleware)` BEFORE `app.use(ratelimit)`, `ctx.state.userId` is already populated by the time the limiter runs, so any account holder has unlimited throughput against expensive endpoints. (3) `blacklist` is present only as commented-out boilerplate. Compounding all of it, the limiter keys on `id: (ctx) => ctx.request.ip || ctx.ip || ctx.state.userId` while index.ts sets `app.proxy = true`, which makes Koa derive `ctx.request.ip` from the client-supplied X-Forwarded-For header — so even the unauthenticated 150/min bucket is trivially evaded by rotating that header.

`ensureIsUUID` in packages/backend/src/utils/ingest.ts carries an explicit self-admission that its validation is incomplete — `if (!id || id.length === 36) return id // TODO: better UUID check` — and accepts ANY 36-character string as a trusted UUID, passing it through unmodified instead of hashing it via uuidFromSeed. Only non-36-char inputs get normalized. This is the identifier validator on the ingest path: `cleanEvent` calls `runId: await ensureIsUUID(runId)` and `parentRunId: await ensureIsUUID(parentRunId)` on attacker-supplied event data, and `/v1/runs/ingest` is in the publicRoutes allowlist (unauthenticated). A 36-char non-UUID runId therefore flows unvalidated into the run insert/update SQL.

`handlePasswordReset` in packages/frontend/pages/update-password.tsx is a stub whose real implementation was removed and replaced with a hardcoded success flag: `// TODO: reset password with supertoken` followed by `const ok = true`. The handler never transmits the new password anywhere — no fetcher/API call exists in the function — yet it unconditionally shows the notification `message: "Password updated successfully"` and then `if (ok) { Router.push("/") }`. A user who believes they have rotated a compromised password has not; the old credential remains valid indefinitely with positive confirmation to the contrary. Note the same file's validator also accepts 5-character passwords (`val.length < 5`) while the sibling reset-password.tsx enforces 6.

New-account email verification can be switched off wholesale by the SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY environment variable, in two coordinated places: packages/backend/src/api/v1/auth/index.ts line 62 inserts accounts with `verified: process.env.SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY ? true : false`, marking them pre-verified, and packages/backend/src/utils/emails.ts line 10 makes sendVerifyEmail `return` immediately so no verification token is ever issued. When set, anyone can self-register an account bound to an email address they do not control, and the `verified` column — the gate other code relies on to distinguish proven from unproven ownership — reports true. Flagged under this shape as a deliberately-provided kill switch for an authentication control rather than an accidental defect; a verifier should confirm whether it is set in deployed/compose configuration.

The input-validation guard on the external-users listing endpoint was commented out rather than deleted, leaving the unbounded query live. `users.get("/", ...)` in packages/backend/src/api/v1/external-users.ts retains the disabled block `// const { limit, page } = ctx.query` / `// if(!limit || !page) { //   return ctx.throw(400, "limit and page are required") // }` plus `// TODO: pagination`, and then runs a SELECT over the whole external_user table for the project with no LIMIT and a correlated per-row aggregate subquery (`(select coalesce(sum(cost), 0) from run where external_user_id = external_user.id) as cost`). Every call forces a full scan plus one aggregate per external user, an unauthenticated-amplification / resource-exhaustion vector given the rate limiter is also neutered (see the ratelimit lead).

packages/frontend/next.config.js ships with both static-analysis build gates deliberately disabled, and the in-repo comments acknowledge the risk in the strongest terms the authors had available: `eslint: { // Warning: This allows production builds to successfully complete even if your project has ESLint errors. ignoreDuringBuilds: true }` and `typescript: { // !! WARN !! // Dangerously allow production builds to successfully complete even if your project has type errors. // !! WARN !! ignoreBuildErrors: true }`. This is not itself an exploitable sink, but it is the mechanism by which the type- and lint-level defects elsewhere in this report (e.g. the dead lowercase `ctx.method === "options"` comparison in cors.ts, and the unvalidated `ctx.state.projectId = bearerToken` assignment) reach production without ever failing a build. Reported as supporting context for this shape.

leads.text: Attacker-controlled regex pattern is compiled and executed server-side: in packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts the CHECK_RUNNERS entry with id="regex" destructures `const { regex, type, field } = params` (line 98) and then builds `const re = new RegExp(regex)` (line 100), running it via `re.test(lastMsg(run[field]))` (line 102) and `run[field].match(re)` (line 106). The pattern text is never length-limited, anchored, or screened for nested quantifiers, so a stored check such as params.regex = "(a+)+$" or "(x*)*y" causes catastrophic backtracking against run input text, hanging the Node event loop (single-threaded DoS). The `params` object is attacker-supplied: runChecks.ts:83 does `params = check.params` and runChecks.ts:98 calls `runner.evaluator!(run, params)`; the check objects come from HTTP bodies at `checklists.post("/")` (checklists.ts:33, `const { slug, type, data } = ctx.request.body`), `checklists.patch("/:id")` (checklists.ts:54), `radars.post("/")` (radars.ts:217, `const { description, view, checks, ... } = ctx.request.body`) and `radars.patch("/:radarId")` (radars.ts:243). The radar cron job then re-runs the stored pattern over many runs (jobs/radar.ts:12 `runChecksOnRun(run, checks, true)`), amplifying the stall.

leads.text: Over-broad regex literal in the authentication allowlist exposes mutating dataset endpoints to unauthenticated callers. packages/backend/src/api/v1/auth/utils.ts:76 adds `new RegExp(`/v1/datasets/.+`)` to `publicRoutes` with the comment "getDataSets in SDKs" (read-only intent), but authMiddleware (line 81) evaluates it as `publicRoutes.some((route) => typeof route === "string" ? route === ctx.path : route.test(ctx.path))` (line 85) with NO HTTP-method discrimination. Because the datasets router is `new Router({prefix: "/datasets"})` (datasets/index.ts:9) mounted on `const v1 = new Router({prefix: "/v1"})` (api/v1/index.ts:18) via `v1.use(datasets.routes())` (api/v1/index.ts:39), the literal matches every dataset sub-route including the destructive ones: `datasets.delete("/:id")` (line 111), `datasets.patch("/:id")` (line 96), `datasets.delete("/prompts/:id")` (line 166), `datasets.patch("/prompts/:id")` (line 176), `datasets.delete("/variations/:id")` (line 202), `datasets.patch("/variations/:variationId")` (line 211), `datasets.post("/prompts")` (line 120), `datasets.post("/variations")` (line 243). authMiddleware then does `if (isPublicRoute && (!bearerToken || validateUUID(bearerToken))) { ... await next(); return }`, skipping verifyJwt entirely. The delete handler compounds this by not scoping to the project at all: `await sql`delete from dataset where id = ${id}``. Failure scenario: an unauthenticated `DELETE /v1/datasets/<uuid>` with no Authorization header matches the regex, bypasses JWT verification, and deletes any tenant's dataset (ctx.status = 200).

All four regex literals in the `publicRoutes` authentication allowlist (packages/backend/src/api/v1/auth/utils.ts lines 63, 71, 72, 76) are missing `^` and `$` anchors, and are consumed with `route.test(ctx.path)` (line 85), which has SUBSTRING semantics — unlike the plain-string entries in the same array, which are compared with strict equality (`route === ctx.path`). The literals are `new RegExp(`/auth/.+`)`, `new RegExp(`/v1/runs/.+/public`)`, `new RegExp(`/v1/runs/.+/feedback`)` and `new RegExp(`/v1/datasets/.+`)`. Consequently ANY request path that merely CONTAINS one of these fragments is classified as public and skips verifyJwt — e.g. a path like `/v1/users/auth/x` or `/v1/orgs/v1/datasets/x` satisfies `isPublicRoute`. `.+` also matches `/`, so the patterns span arbitrarily many path segments rather than one. This makes the allowlist's blast radius depend on route-table coincidences instead of an explicit list, and any future route whose path embeds `/auth/` or `/v1/datasets/` silently becomes unauthenticated. Anchoring each literal (`^/v1/datasets/[^/]+$`) and splitting by HTTP method is the fix.

No runtime third-party component is declared with a version, even though the code demonstrably requires many security-relevant runtime packages — `require("koa")`, `require("koa-bodyparser")`, `require("koa-router")`, `require("koa-ratelimit")`, `require("@koa/cors")`, `require("jose")`/`jose.jwtVerify`, `require("bcrypt")`, `require("argon2")`, `require("openai")`, `require("litellm")`, `require("prexit")` and Stripe. This is a coverage gap to resolve with a real manifest/lockfile SCA pass, not an asserted CVE — I am explicitly NOT claiming any of the 5 declared packages is vulnerable.
